title: C# AnimationPlayers are incredibly inefficient
body:
### Tested versions

Tested on 4.4.dev1 & 4.6 stable (same results on both)

### System information

Godot v4.6.stable.mono - macOS Tahoe (26.2.0) - Multi-window, 1 monitor - Vulkan (Forward+) - dedicated AMD Radeon Pro 5700 XT - Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-10910 CPU @ 3.60GHz (20 threads) - 32.00 GiB memory

### Issue description

Animation players are really slow and inefficient in general. I've included an example in the minimal reproduction project. It has 10 tracks, 4 "Visible" properties, 2 hitbox "Disabled" properties, 1 position and 3 boolean exports.

On my system, it takes 20-30 microseconds to process when nothing is happening (seems a little high, but whatever).
It takes over 1000 microseconds to "Play" an animation (triggered when pressing the "A" key). This seems crazy - setting the same flags the animation player sets with its tracks in code instead takes only a few dozen microseconds (excluding time to toggle hitboxes, which is also a few dozen).
While the animation is playing, it takes 200-500 microseconds to process (advance) the animation. Considering the track values aren't changing at all during this time, this also seems absurd - it's up to 500 microseconds to do absolutely nothing.

And strangest of all, from my tests it seems that the microsecond duration of operations depends not just on how many tracks there are, but on how many animations there are?! Why does having more animations on an animation player degrade performance when they're not even the ones being played?

This is all for one animation player with some basic tracks. Animation players are a common tool used by many different scenes - so widely used because they are so generally useful. The fact that just 16 of them can together take all the processing time you have for a frame - or more - is absurd.

I've recently been optimizing my early access indie game and this is the main culprit of performance. Most of the ways I can optimize things are just by reducing my reliance on animation players, which sucks considering how useful they are. Even implementing a simplified animation player in C# code can save hundreds of microseconds.

I don't expect animation players to be the most efficient things in the world, nor as fast as setting properties directly in code. But this seems rather silly in its current state. I should be able to use animation players for normal things without worrying about butchering my game's performance in the process.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open the minimal reproduction project
2. If opening in >4.4-dev1, convert the project automatically
3. Run the project
4. Output should start appearing in the output log. Each line is a microsecond count of an operation
5. Press "A" on the keyboard. This will play an animation and output an additional line with a microsecond count of how long it took to play the animation
6. Quit the program and observe the output log

### Minimal reproduction project (MRP)

[AnimationPlayerPerformanceMRP.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24924647/AnimationPlayerPerformanceMRP.zip)
